articles.title: There's reason to believe the private sector economy is actually doing pretty well
articles.text:
Private sector economy looks fairly strong, latest PMI shows
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 23, 2026
There's reason to believe the private sector economy is actually doing pretty well
S&P Global Market Intelligence’s purchasing managers’ index signaled strong, sustained economic growth in October.
Economyby Mitchell Hartman
Download
halbergman/Getty Images
Whatever else in the economic firmament might be giving you agita — stocks, bonds, oil prices, uncertainty and volatility in all of the above — the private-sector economy is actually doing, “really very well, thank you.”
S&P Global Market Intelligence’s purchasing managers' index, which is based on a survey of manufacturing and service-sector companies, signaled strong, sustained economic growth in October. It also reported a pick-up in hiring plans and solid new-order flow and production levels.
There’s still one big warning sign flashing red: inflation. The prices for the stuff companies buy and sell keep surging higher.
Still, the growth of U.S. business activity remained near a five-year high in October, said economist Chris Williamson at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
“This is another really strong report in terms of manufacturing growth, accompanied by service-sector growth as well, it’s a broad-based upturn that we’ve got,” he said.
It’s a welcome change from the past few years for manufacturing, which was hit hard by tariffs and the Trump administration’s trade wars.
“For so long in manufacturing we saw dormant activity, and that has picked up quite nicely, said Nationwide Chief Economist Kathy Bostjancic.
She has two letters for what’s driving this: “AI. [It’s] boosting both manufacturing and construction. We know the construction sector could use that because residential housing continues to be in the dumpster.”
Still, rampant price growth is not so favorable for the economy, said Williamson at S&P. “We’ve got prices charged for goods and services rising at the fastest rate for four years, well above the [Federal Reserve’s] target,” he said.
So far though, corporate America is rolling with it.
“Companies are seeing their costs increase — notably fuel and energy — but they’re able to pass that on to their customers,” Williamson said, without squeezing their profit margins
And, without driving consumers away, said Dan North, senior economist at credit-insurer Allianz Trade.
“Consumers [have] been driving the economy, despite terrible sentiment, and disposable personal income slowing down pretty sharply,” he said.
North said the consumers who drive the most spending — the top 20% by income — aren’t really daunted by high prices, because of all the wealth they’ve banked from housing and the stock market.

articles.title: Open enrollment is here and the cost of employer health plans is going up — again
articles.text:
Employer-sponsored health insurance costs are climbing — again
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 23, 2026
Open enrollment is here and the cost of employer health plans is going up — again
Premiums for employer-sponsored health insurance rose 9% this year, with families paying more than $7,000 on average for coverage, according to a new KFF survey.
Healthcareby Samantha Fields
Download
The average deductible for one person is now almost $2,000.
fstop123/Getty Images
If you are in the majority of people under 65 who get health insurance through an employer, you’ve probably noticed it’s getting more expensive.
Premiums for people with employer-sponsored insurance rose 9% this year, on average, according to a new survey from the health policy nonprofit KFF. All indications are they’re on track to rise again next year.
We are heading into open enrollment season, that time of year when you sign up for health insurance.
“Everywhere you look, costs are going up this year,” said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor at Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms.
Most people with employer-sponsored coverage can expect to see higher premiums next year, especially if they work for smaller companies, she said.
More on healthcare costs
From Oct. 16: Earlier screening for financial aid in hospitals could help lower bills
From Oct. 9: How a law to protect patients from surprise billing shifted the cost to employers
From Sept. 18: Having insurance is not a guarantee against medical debt, survey finds
“If they're lucky enough to have a choice of more than one plan, they may be able to shift to a lower cost plan, but often that will come with downsides, like a narrower network or a higher deductible,” she said.
Employer-sponsored insurance has long been the backbone of the U.S. healthcare system. “But that backbone is really starting to crumble,” said Corlette.
It’s not just monthly premiums that are rising; many employers are also raising co-pays and deductibles, making it more expensive to actually go to the doctor.
All of this is presenting a real challenge for many people, said Matthew Rae, the associate director of the Program on the Health Care Marketplace at the health policy nonprofit KFF.
“If you're in a family health insurance plan, on average, you're spending over $7,000 to enroll in coverage,” he said.
And the average deductible for one person is now almost $2,000.
“Many people with job-based coverage don't have the savings to meet those levels of deductibles,” he said. Which means, increasingly, even people who have insurance feel like they can’t afford to use it.
It's not just healthcare costs that are going up

articles.title: Heating oil prices are up 70%, just as Northeast residents fill up for winter
articles.text:
Heating oil prices up 70% as Northeast residents fill up for winter
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 22, 2026
Heating oil prices are up 70%, just as Northeast residents fill up for winter
Heating oil is used in just 3% of U.S. homes, but most of those are in the Northeast. Spiking prices mean residents and heating oil delivery companies are facing a challenging winter ahead.
Energyby Henry Epp
Download
Todd Lavalley drives a heating oil delivery truck for Gillespie Fuels & Propane in central Vermont. Delivery companies face higher diesel costs, along with customers facing a spike in heating oil prices.
Henry Epp/Marketplace
People who heat their home with heating oil could spend 21% more this winter to stay warm, according to the Energy Information Administration.
Just 3% of U.S. homes rely on heating oil, and most of them are concentrated in the Northeast. As the weather turns colder, Northeast residents and the companies that deliver heating oil in the region are already trying to navigate much higher costs.
Getting a heating oil delivery is a little like having a gas pump pull up to your house in a 3,000-gallon tanker truck. Todd Lavalley drives one for Gillespie Fuels and Propane in central Vermont. About a third of homes in the state heat with oil.
On a rainy Tuesday morning, Lavalley steered his truck into a customer’s driveway in the town of Berlin, pulled a red hose about the diameter of the fat end of a baseball bat up the driveway, clamped it to a pipe on the side of the house, turned a lever, and oil began flowing.
Unlike at a gas station, there’s no automatic shutoff when the tank is full. Instead, Lavalley has to listen for a high-pitched whistling sound to die down.
“When that stops, that’s how we know it’s full,” he said. “That’s the only way we know it’s full. If you miss, and you don’t shut it off, you have a mess.”
He’s had a few messes in his over 20 years of delivering heating oil, but they don’t happen too often. It’s especially important not to spill any when the stuff costs over $6 per gallon, a record high.
“It is diesel fuel,” said Matt Cota, a lobbyist who represents heating oil delivery companies in Vermont. Like diesel, heating oil prices have been driven up by refinery outages caused by wars across the globe.
More on energy costs
From Oct. 8: Here's where home heating will cost more this winter
From Sept. 22: How global disruptions are impacting heating oil prices
From Sept. 14: Diesel fuel hit a record high. Unlike gas, using less of it is not an option
High prices are squeezing both residents and the companies that deliver the fuel. For delivery companies, higher prices cut into their profits, in part, because their tanker trucks run on diesel.
“When you see higher prices, you see lower margins, you see higher transportation costs, and you see longer times from when the consumer receives the fuel to when they can pay,” Cota said.
For East Coast residents, a gallon of heating oil costs about 70% more than it did this time last year — though not all residents will pay that price. Some customers arranged for their fuel deliveries back in the summer. That essentially allowed them to make a bet that fuel prices were going to go up, locking in a price of around $4 per gallon.
“In hindsight, that looks like a pretty good deal, but not everyone can take advantage of it, or not everyone thought it was a good deal at the time,” Cota said.
High prices this fall are also prompting more people than usual to reach out to fuel assistance programs. Close to $4 billion from the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance program is headed to states. In Vermont, that money, coupled with state funds, won’t be released to residents for a few more weeks, said Sue Rossi, the outreach director at Capstone Community Action in central Vermont. But already, people are calling the poverty relief nonprofit about it.
At Capstone Community Action in Barre, Vermont, outreach workers are already receiving a higher number of calls from residents looking for heating assistance.
Henry Epp/Marketplace
“More people than ever are inquiring about, ‘When is fuel assistance?’” Rossi said. “That happens every year, but not only ‘When is it?’ but ‘How much is it?’ They want to know.”
For now, she doesn’t have answers. But for the neediest clients, she can offer help. Capstone Community Action runs its own fuel assistance program funded by private donations. Because of the high demand, Rossi said the nonprofit started giving out money about a month earlier than last year.
“The people we're actually helping is a… smaller amount of who's calling, but we're doing that on purpose to just get the ones that seem the most needy, most vulnerable, to hold them over.”
The maximum available to a resident, Rossi says, is $500. But with prices so high, the agency is considering increasing that limit as the season goes on.

articles.title: What do we owe our families?
articles.text:
What do we owe our families?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Subscribe:
Apple

Oct 22, 2026
What do we owe our families?
Balancing your own financial needs and the pressure to provide.
Download
Financial therapist Sahaj Kaur Kohli (left) and financial educator Gigi Gonzalez (right).
Kohli's photo by Beowulf Sheehan | Gonzalez's photo courtesy guest.
Subscribe:
Apple
Spotify
Amazon
RSS
Do you feel pressure to provide financially for your immigrant parents? Children of immigrants are more likely to be parentified, whether that’s by helping out financially or translating paperwork. And that feeling of obligation can carry through adulthood. This week, host Reema Khrais asks: what do first-generation Americans owe their families, and how do we balance caring for parents with caring for ourselves?
Khrais talks with Gigi Gonzalez, financial educator and author of “Cultura y Cash,” and Sahaj Kaur Kohli, therapist and author of “But What Will People Say?”
Key ideas:
Gonzalez’ “quiero y puedo” framework: Do you want to help? And are you able to?
Thriver’s guilt: Children of immigrants may feel guilt for having access to more resources, opportunities and choices than their parents.
Reciprocal vs authoritarian filial piety: One’s feelings of loyalty to your parents can be shaped by internal (“I want to be able to do this for my parents”) or external (“I need to”) motivations.
Collectivist vs. individualist culture: A collectivist culture prioritizes family and community, sometimes at the expense of the individual; whereas an individualistic culture prioritizes the individual, sometimes at the expense of others.
Bicultural straddling: First-generation Americans can face the challenge of constant adaptation between two cultural influences.
Khrais posed a few real-life scenarios for Gonzalez and Kohli. Here is their advice (lightly edited for clarity and length):
Question 1: You're dating someone from a different cultural background, and you feel responsible for financially helping your parents, but your partner resents that you're prioritizing them over your future together. How do you recommend people navigate that?
Gonzalez: My husband is half Mexican and half white, but he was raised culturally white, so he still questions that. I recently visited my grandmother in Mexico, and I had the cash to give her $500 – I wanted to and I could. And my husband’s like, “Why, Giovanna?” Because I want to, that's why! And because I can.
Kohli: I'm a cross-cultural couples therapist, so I literally work with couples where one is often American, either white or Black, and then the other partner is usually a child of an immigrant. I'm also married to a white American man. And when we think about this question, it’s not really about the money – it’s more about family values. It's more about how much should family be involved? How much should we be involved?
These are questions that we should be having with our partners very early on. When my husband and I were dating very early on, we had very explicit conversations around culture, religion, family, expectations, norms, all of these things, and he was on board from the beginning. And if he wasn't, we wouldn't be together. And I think these are the conversations we need to have, and money is a part of that.
Question 2: What if you're in a big family and you're not on the same page about this stuff with your siblings? Let’s say your brothers don’t feel the need to help out your aging parents, so you’re stuck with dealing with it alone. How do you approach that?
Gonzalez: I've seen this play out with my aunts and uncles, with my grandparents. There's five adult children, and you think between five working, able-bodied working adults, there wouldn't be an issue to provide a monthly allowance for their parents! But there is an issue, because they have their own families and financial goals, and some contribute more than others. There's definitely some resentment that's built amongst them. I see that happening, and that's why I started conversations with my brothers early.
Kohli: When I hear that the siblings aren't on the same page, I want to know what's the dynamic at play and why? There’s a family systems thing happening here: each sibling, depending on birth order, gender, lifestyle, favoritism, etc. All these things will impact the way someone feels either more reciprocity with their parents, versus like this burden of having to, and then wanting to opt out and saying, “Screw this, I'm not going to, I can't do this.” So there's more at play here: Money is emotional, and there's a lot of stories that we're taught about money, but also family dynamics.
And so when I hear a sibling wants to opt out, for me, there's a curiosity of why: what happened that has caused you to feel like you don't want to support anymore? If you're the sibling who's frustrated, how do you approach that? Not from a place of “you need to help, I'm alone in this,” but rather in terms of: “What's going on with you? I want to understand more about where you're coming from.” So many of us aren't taught to have these direct, explicit conversations, but we need to.
Question 3: What if your parents don’t need your support, but you still feel cultural pressure to give?
Khrais: Just to use an example in my own life, my parents visited me in Portland, and I ended up just for ease, booking their tickets and their Airbnb because, logistically, it was simpler. And so they eventually asked me to Venmo-request them. And I’ve been going back and forth in my head, I’m like, should I send the Venmo request?
Kohli: I think if you are giving to your parents because you feel a pressure that you have to, and you feel like if you don’t they might say something and there’s this kind of implicit, unsaid obligation there again, the therapist in me is going to ask why? articles.title: Has the recipe for Reese's changed? It depends on how you define "change"
articles.text:
Why Reese's don't taste like they used to
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 22, 2026
Has the recipe for Reese's changed? It depends on how you define "change"
Rachel Handler, features writer at New York Magazine, investigated how the taste of Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups has changed over time.
Cultureby Kai Ryssdal and Sean McHenry
Download
“The thing is that Hershey, they care to the extent that people notice, but as long as people are still buying it, they don't care," Handler said.
Jc Milhet/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
For Rachel Handler, features writer at Vulture and New York Magazine, her investigation into Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups started after Brad Reese, the grandson of Reese’s inventor, complained about the chocolate on LinkedIn.
“When I when I first started talking to him, he was like, ‘I used to eat a Reese's cup every single day of my life,’” said Handler. “And he just came out swinging on and basically said, you know, this doesn't taste the same anymore.”
Hershey did admit to changing the recipe, according to the Associated Press, but maintained the identity of the cups was unchanged.
Handler consulted chocolate expert Beth Kimmerle, who reconstructed several historical Reese’s recipes to taste compare to the modern candy you can find on the shelf. And while today’s recipe was ultimately found wanting, the results weren’t totally conclusive. At one point during the test, Handler confused the modern recipe with the original.
“I felt really cocky,” said Handler. “I just was like, ‘OK, yeah, this is definitely one of the originals,’ but I was wrong and I thought that was fascinating. I think I think we've been trained as consumers to not to trust ourselves, not to trust our palates, not to trust our own experience.”
“Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal spoke with Handler about her reporting.

The horror genre isn't limited to Halloween anymore
Marketplace®

Donate

Horror is good business — not just during Halloween
Andrew Webster, entertainment editor at The Verge, explains why horror movies, games and TV shows are gaining attention and prestige across the media landscape.
Cultureby Kai Ryssdal and Mika Ellison
Download
Film studios and gaming companies are starting to bet more on horror films, which are cheaper to make and draw crowds.
Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures
Horror isn’t just for Halloween anymore. Streaming sites like Netflix and Amazon Prime are betting on horror movies. Games like Resident Evil are incredibly popular. The horror-comedy TV show “Widow’s Bay” broke records during awards season.
Andrew Webster is entertainment editor at The Verge. He recently explored why horror is such good business right now, and why it’s gotten so big lately.
“As things have just gotten so much more expensive in games and film” Webster said, “making a movie that costs $10 million — like ‘Backrooms’ — and has the potential to make half a billion dollars, is a much better bet than throwing a couple hundred million dollars at Steven Spielberg.”
“Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal spoke with Webster about his reporting.

articles.title: AI (still) has the publishing industry in a tizzy
articles.text:
The publishing industry's AI battle
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 20, 2026
AI (still) has the publishing industry in a tizzy
“What publishers and literary agents are struggling with behind the scenes is what percentage of AI assistance crosses the line into, ‘we could lose more money than we stand to make,’” publishing journalist Jane Friedman said.
Cultureby Kai Ryssdal and Sean McHenry
Download
AI has faced more pushback in creative industries like publishing, where consumers are more averse to artificially generated content.
Alex Kent/The Washington Post via Getty Images
Generative AI has been increasingly adopted across many industries, like scientific research and informational services. But in creative industries like book publishing, the story is a little different.
Jane Friedman is a journalist who covers the publishing industry and has created an FAQ resource on publishing and AI. She has a few words to describe how people in the publishing world are feeling right now.
“Confusing, overwhelming, anger-inducing,” she said. “Pick the negative emotion. It's one of those.”
Earlier this year, several book releases were canceled after allegations that the books were composed with the help of AI. At the same time, publishers themselves are using AI behind the scenes.
“The biggest publishers all have said they're using AI in some way, shape, or form behind the scenes for their own business operations,” Friedman said. “But at the same time, they are saying, ‘We want to protect human creativity and authors.’ And everyone's trying not to offend the general public or the readership who are, I think it's fair to say, not well-disposed to AI.”
“Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal spoke to Friedman about the state of AI and publishing.
To listen to their conversation, use the “play” button at the top of this page.
